The MOMENTUM 5 Wireless still supports **aptX Lossless**, which is a meaningful feature on paper and potentially in practice. But the BTD 700 experience needs that fix before I would call it a slam dunk. Great concept. Right now, a little too much gremlin in the machine.

## Listening

![sennheiser-momentum-5-wireless-headphones-earcups](https://www.ecoustics.com/wp-content/uploads/sennheiser-momentum-5-wireless-headphones-earcups.jpg)

MOMENTUM 5 earcups

The MOMENTUM 5 Wireless and HDB 630 are cut from the same Sennheiser cloth, and anyone expecting two completely different headphones is going to be disappointed. Or relieved. They share a lot of the same DNA: excellent clarity, a largely linear tonal balance, strong midrange presence, and a presentation that favors detail and space over cheap bass tricks. Sennheiser did not turn the MOMENTUM 5 into a skull-rattling gym headphone, and thank you for small mercies.

But there are differences, and they matter.

Where the **HDB 630** leans a little more restrained and studio-minded, the **MOMENTUM 5 Wireless** brings slightly more weight and impact in the bass range. It still will not rearrange your dental work, but there is more definition, punch, and low-end authority than I heard from the HDB 630. Green Day’s “Jesus of Suburbia” and “21 Guns” still had the clarity, imaging, and sense of space that made the HDB 630 so easy to like, but the MOMENTUM 5 added a little more drive underneath the guitars and drums. Not bloated. Not boosted into stupidity. Just more physical.

That difference became more obvious with Daft Punk’s “Get Lucky” and “Giorgio by Moroder.” The HDB 630 presents those tracks with a more open, almost studio-monitor sense of space, which is rare for a closed-back wireless headphone. The MOMENTUM 5 does not lose that Sennheiser clarity, but it adds more rhythmic grip and bass definition. The groove lands with more conviction, which matters when the entire point of the track is to make you forget whatever nonsense you were supposed to be doing for the next six minutes. ![Sennheiser HDB 630 Wireless Headphones with Travel Case](https://www.ecoustics.com/wp-content/uploads/sennheiser-hdb-630-with-case.jpg)

Sennheiser HDB 630 Wireless Headphones with Travel Case

Sia’s “Unstoppable,” “Cheap Thrills,” and “Breathe Me” pushed the MOMENTUM 5 in a different direction. Those tracks are a cheerful little reminder that love, betrayal, and emotional wreckage can apparently come with solid production values. Her voice was cleanly centered and easy to follow, with enough texture to keep the emotional weight intact. “Breathe Me” in particular exposed the MOMENTUM 5’s ability to keep vocals intimate without turning the presentation syrupy. The HDB 630 is a touch more controlled and refined through the upper ranges, but the MOMENTUM 5 gives the material a bit more body.

Massive Attack’s “Teardrop” also favored the MOMENTUM 5’s extra bass definition. The pulsing low end had more shape and authority than it does through the HDB 630, while the vocal remained suspended in the mix with that slightly ghostly quality the track needs. Again, this is not bass-head territory. Sennheiser is not auditioning for a parking lot SPL contest. But the MOMENTUM 5 has more impact where the HDB 630 can sometimes feel a little polite.

Disturbed’s cover of “The Sound of Silence” was the track that really exposed the difference. David Draiman’s voice needs weight, control, and scale, and the MOMENTUM 5 gave it more physical presence than the HDB 630. The power in his delivery hit harder, especially as the arrangement builds. Draiman is also a total mensch and a personal hero, so I am not exactly coming into that track emotionally neutral. Still, the MOMENTUM 5 handled the vocal intensity well without smearing the edges or turning the whole thing into melodrama with Bluetooth attached.

The one tradeoff is the top end. On some of the same tracks I used with the HDB 630, the MOMENTUM 5 Wireless sounded slightly harder through the treble. Not bright enough to become a deal-breaker, and not sharp enough to make me start bargaining with my own ears, but it is there. The HDB 630 has a little more refinement and composure up top, while the MOMENTUM 5 trades some of that smoothness for greater bass impact and a more energetic overall presentation.

That is really the comparison in one sentence: the **[HDB 630](https://www.ecoustics.com/reviews/sennheiser-hdb-630/)** is the more restrained, refined, audiophile-leaning wireless headphone, while the **MOMENTUM 5 Wireless** gets very close in clarity and tonal balance but adds more bass definition, more punch, and a little more everyday fun. Sennheiser may have created a problem for itself here, because the less expensive headphone does not sound like the lesser one in every category.

![sennheiser-momentum-5-wireless-headphones-black-angle](https://www.ecoustics.com/wp-content/uploads/sennheiser-momentum-5-wireless-headphones-black-angle.jpg)

MOMENTUM 5

## The Bottom Line

The **Sennheiser MOMENTUM 5 Wireless** is not a dramatic reinvention, but it does not need to be. The upgrades that matter are practical and audible: **Dolby Atmos with head tracking**, stronger ANC with **four microphones per side**, **aptX Lossless**, **Hi-Res Audio certification**, an **8-band EQ**, and a **user-replaceable 700 mAh battery**. That battery is the sleeper feature because it gives the $399.99 MOMENTUM 5 a real longevity advantage in a category where too many brands still treat worn-out batteries as your problem.

What is missing? There is still **[no LDAC](https://www.ecoustics.com/articles/ldac-aptx-aac-sbc-bluetooth/)**, the **BTD 700 dongle issue needs a fix**, and the MOMENTUM 5 does not include the same accessory package as the more expensive **HDB 630**. It also does not feel quite as premium as the **[Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3](https://www.ecoustics.com/reviews/bowers-wilkins-px7-s3-wireless-anc-headphones/)** or **[Px8 S2](https://www.ecoustics.com/reviews/bowers-wilkins-px8-s2-wireless-headphones/)**, even if the build is solid, comfortable, and travel-friendly.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Should you buy it over the HDB 630 and save some money? For many listeners, yes. The HDB 630 still has the more refined, audiophile-leaning presentation, but the MOMENTUM 5 gets surprisingly close while offering stronger bass impact, excellent ANC, a better travel footprint, and a lower price. That makes it one of the more compelling wireless headphones in the **$350 to $450** range, and anyone shopping there should put it on the audition list before Sony, Bose, Apple, or Bowers get the automatic nod.

### Pros:

* Strong clarity, detail retrieval, and linear tonal balance
* More bass impact and definition than the HDB 630, without turning into a bass-heavy mess
* Excellent ANC performance that does not seriously damage sound quality
* Smart Control Plus app is comprehensive, reliable, and genuinely useful
* Adjustable ANC, Anti-Wind mode, multipoint connectivity, and customizable app tiles
* Dolby Atmos support worked properly with TIDAL during testing
* aptX Lossless support gives it a stronger codec story than many rivals
* User-replaceable 700 mAh battery is a major long-term ownership win
* Real-world battery life remains excellent, even if below the claimed maximum
* Lightweight, comfortable fit with solid build quality
* Folds flat and comes with a noticeably smaller travel case than the HDB 630
* Strong value at $399.99 compared with the more expensive HDB 630

### Cons:

* No LDAC support
* BTD 700 USB-C dongle produced distortion with iPhone and MacBook during testing
* Head tracking was not enabled during the review period
* Treble can sound slightly harder than the HDB 630 on some tracks
* Does not feel as premium as the Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 or Px8 S2
* Ear pads could be slightly firmer
* Pads get warm after about 30 minutes
* Does not include the airplane adapter or BTD 700 USB Adapter like the HDB 630
* Touch controls work, but remembering every tap, swipe, pinch, and gesture remains a pain

args.summary:
The Sennheiser MOMENTUM 5 Wireless headphones ($399.99) were reviewed on ecoustics.com by Ian White. Available in Black, White, and Denim from June 16, 2026, these headphones build on the MOMENTUM 4 platform with key upgrades: Dolby Atmos with head tracking (via day-one firmware update), aptX Lossless, Bluetooth 5.4 (upgradable to 6.0), Hi-Res Audio certification, stronger ANC with four microphones per side, an 8-band EQ in the Smart Control Plus app, and a user-replaceable 700 mAh battery—a major longevity advantage. Real-world battery life tested at 51-54 hours with ANC (vs. claimed 57-60 hours). The headphones use the same 42mm transducers as the MOMENTUM 4, with tuning inspired by the HD 600 series.

Sound quality is described as having excellent clarity, linear tonal balance, strong midrange, and more bass impact and definition than the more expensive HDB 630, though the treble can sound slightly harder on some tracks. ANC performance is strong without seriously damaging sound quality. The case is 20% smaller than the HDB 630's. Build quality is solid but less premium than Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3/Px8 S2.

The review compares the MOMENTUM 5 favorably against the HDB 630, noting the MOMENTUM 5 is the more "fun" and bass-forward option while the HDB 630 is more refined and audiophile-leaning. The BTD 700 USB-C dongle had distortion issues with iPhone and MacBook during testing (Sennheiser working on a fix). No LDAC support is included. The reviewer concludes the MOMENTUM 5 is one of the most compelling wireless headphones in the $350-$450 range, offering strong value that may undercut Sennheiser's own HDB 630.

# Sennheiser MOMENTUM 5 Wireless launch with replaceable battery, aptX Lossless, and improved ANC

A worthy challenger to Sony, Bose, and Apple.

By

•

May 25, 2026 — 6:00 PM ET

•

•

[Follow us on Google Discover](https://soundg.co/discoversource "Follow us on Google Discover")[Add us as preferred source](https://soundg.co/googlesource "Add us as preferred source")

TL;DR

* Sennheiser’s MOMENTUM 5 Wireless arrives June 16 at $399.99 USD in Black, White, and Denim
* Features a user-replaceable battery with up to 57 hours of playback with ANC on.
* Ships with Bluetooth 5.4 but will receive BT 6.0 via a future firmware update.

The [MOMENTUM 4 Wireless](https://www.soundguys.com/sennheiser-momentum-4-wireless-review-2-86111/) has spent the last few years as one of the best alternatives to Sony or Bose. They have great sound, absurd battery life, and a price that undercuts the competition. The one knock was always ANC, which didn’t quite match up. With the MOMENTUM 5, Sennheiser is fixing that, adding a ton more, and making a stronger case than ever for the top spot for [flagship wireless headphones](https://www.soundguys.com/best-headphones-2559/).

The headphones themselves look pretty much the same as the previous Momentum 4, with a lay-flat-only design and some new, nice metal accents. It would have been nice if the headphones could fold up for portability, but at least they come with a smaller, fairly robust carrying case for when you are taking them on the go. In particular, I really like the new indentation on the backside that serves as a handle for carrying them.

Under the hood, the MOMENTUM 5 doubles the mic count dedicated to ANC and transparency to four per side, which Sennheiser claims provides up to three times more effective reduction of ambient voice chatter compared to the MOMENTUM 4. We’re really excited to put that to the test in our lab. Call quality should improve too, particularly in windier, noisier environments. The doubled mic array should help deliver more natural voice reproduction on calls and improve overall handling.

The headphones house the same 42mm transducer from its predecessor, tuned in the tradition of the brand’s HD 600-series headphones. This generation adds Hi-Res Audio certification and Snapdragon Sound support, including aptX Lossless, which is a big addition. When paired with compatible devices, that means you’ll enjoy CD-quality audio over Bluetooth with little to no compression artifacts. The Smart Control Plus companion app also gets a new 8-band custom equalizer alongside a Sound Personalization feature that adjusts the frequency response to your hearing profile.

Plush ear pads and a padded headband prioritize long-listening comfort.

Claiming a whopping 57 hours of playback with ANC on, the MOMENTUM 5 pretty much sets a new standard for headphone battery life. But if that wasn’t impressive enough, the 700 mAh battery is also user-replaceable, which is a big win for repairability. It’s a feature that’s still frustratingly uncommon in premium wireless headphones, where sealed designs are the norm, and it’s a meaningful durability argument for a $400 purchase. Sennheiser is selling you a headphone built to last, not one you’ll need to replace after a few years of use.

The headphones ship with Bluetooth 5.4 out of the box but are built to support Bluetooth 6.0 via a future firmware update, which will also bring Dolby Atmos with head-tracking. No confirmed date yet for when that will be. The MOMENTUM 5 Wireless launches June 16 in Black, White, and Denim for $399.99 USD / $569.95 CAD.

URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ORbaKZhb1iE

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a transcript of a YouTube video review of the Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones, posted on May 15, 2026, by RecordingNOW. The reviewer has owned the XM6 for one year and provides an updated assessment, comparing it against the AirPods Max 2 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2.

**Comfort (8.5/10):** The XM6 is very lightweight at 252.8g, but has strong clamping force from the factory (loosens after ~1 month). The ear cups are shallow, causing ears to press against the fabric. The Bose QC Ultra 2 is more comfortable.

**Features, Build Quality, Battery Life, Practicality (9.0/10):** Supports LDAC codec and 10-band custom EQ. Includes a premium foldable hard shell case (reverted from XM5's non-foldable design). Battery life is 30 hours with ANC on, 40 hours off. Build quality feels cheap for a $450 flagship, but the hinge has a metal reinforcement piece to address XM5's broken hinge issue. No wear after one year. Effective multi-point connectivity. The "cinema mode" spatial audio is a standout feature for TV/movies.

**Noise Cancelling (10/10):** Tied with AirPods Max 2 as best-in-class. Better than Bose QC Ultra 2. Very effective across frequencies, minimal white noise/hiss. The strong clamping force helps create a consistent physical seal. Transparency mode is good but not as natural as AirPods Max 2.

**Sound Quality (8.7/10):** The reviewer downgraded the score after a year. Stock sound profile is warm, dark, muddy, flat, and narrow in soundstage. It improves with LDAC and EQ. It's the least favorite among the XM6, AirPods Max 2, Bose QC Ultra 2, and Sennheiser Momentum 4. Bass is impactful when tuned. Cinema mode enhances sub-bass. The reviewer does not reach for the XM6 for pure music listening.

**Value (8.0/10):** Retails at $458 USD, often seen around $428, and as low as $399 on sale. Priced fairly for its best-in-class ANC, but build quality and sound quality lag behind similarly priced competitors like the Bowers & Wilkins PX7 S3 and Sennheiser Momentum 4 (often under $250).

**Overall Score:** 8.9/10. The reviewer uses the XM6 almost daily for its cinema mode and ANC. It is considered one of the best all-around daily driver and travel headphones on the market, despite comfort and sound quality shortcomings.
</summary>

args.summary:
EL JEFE REVIEWS published a video review (March 7, 2026) of the Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds after 3 weeks of daily use. The reviewer tested review samples provided by Sony (not sponsored). Key findings:

**Battery Life**: Sony claimed 8 hours with ANC on, but real-world testing with LDAC at 60-75% volume yielded only 6-6.5 hours. Competitors like Technics AZ100 push 10+ hours. Quick charge: 3 minutes gives 60 minutes of play. IPX4 water resistance.

**Design & Comfort**: 10% smaller than XM5s, sit deeper/flush in ear. Stock polyurethane foam tips create excellent ANC seal but can cause ear pressure, heat, and itchiness. The reviewer recommends third-party silicone tips (e.g., SpinFit Omni) for better comfort, though ANC drops ~10%.

**Sound Quality**: Improved clarity over XM5—more open and airy. Bass is heavy/boomy stock but can be tuned via EQ. Vocals are forward and textured. Treble is very detailed/high-energy but can be fatiguing for long sessions. The reviewer considers these the most lively earbuds in class compared to AirPods Pro 3 and Technics AZ100.

**ANC & Transparency**: ANC is "S-tier," best in class, deleting low frequencies (fans, motors, engines). Transparency mode is improved over XM5 (~95-97% of AirPods Pro 3) but still feels like wearing microphones.

**Deal Breakers**: (1) Foam tips degrade and get grimy over time; (2) Missing flagship features—no find-my-speaker, no LE Audio, no Auracast; (3) Multipoint limited to 2 devices (Technics supports 3); (4) Gaming latency noticeable in competitive shooters; (5) Ghost touches due to smaller shell.

**Verdict**: The hype was mostly real, but $329 is too expensive. The reviewer recommends waiting for discounts to ~$250. At $300, AirPods Pro 3 are the safer bet for longevity. The XM6 are the kings of ANC but have notable shortcomings in battery life, features, and comfort.

## Table of Contents

Sony's latest flagship audio product, the [WF-1000XM6 earbuds](https://mashable.com/review/sony-wf-1000xm6-earbuds), is officially here as of Feb. 12.

Just like last year's [XM6 headphones](https://mashable.com/article/sony-xm6-headphones-launch-price), these earbuds feature better active noise cancellation, improved sound quality, and an upgraded design. Also like their headphones counterpart, those updates come at a cost — Sony bumped up the starting price to $329.99, which is $30 more than the release price of the [WF-1000XM5 earbuds](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/sony-electronics-unveils-wf-1000xm5-truly-wireless-earbuds-for-the-music-the-best-noise-canceling-earbuds-301883612.html "(opens in a new window)") released three years ago.

After spending a week [testing out the earbuds](https://mashable.com/review/sony-wf-1000xm6-earbuds), I can see why Sony raised the price point — they're some of the most well-rounded [noise-cancelling earbuds](https://mashable.com/roundup/best-noise-cancelling-earbuds) I've ever tried. Still, $329.99 is no small chunk of change, so to help you make any purchasing decisions, I've broken down what's new, what's the same, and where to pick up Sony's latest release.

## Sony WF-1000XM6: The specs

![sony xm6 earbuds case open with one left earbud in the case](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/05AGLIYBYN3gt692vZMsmtc/images-2.fill.size_2000x1124.v1770849309.jpg)

The XM6 come with a redesigned case and earbud shape. Credit: Joe Maldonado / Mashable

So what do you get for $329.99? Here's the basic breakdown:

* **Processor:** QN3e
* **Equalizer:** 10-band custom equalizer with app
* **Battery life:** 8 hours per charge, 24 hours with case
* **Microphones:** 8 mics
* **IP rating:** IPX4
* **Charging:** USB-C and Qi wireless charging
* **Bluetooth codecs:** SBC/AAC/LDAC/LC3
* **Ear tips:** XS, S, M, L
* **Colors:** Platinum silver, black

If you've been [paying attention to the recent leaks](https://mashable.com/article/sony-xm6-earbuds-leak-specs-price), these specs won't be a surprise. The headline is that these buds offer a zippier performance thanks to the new QN3e chip and better noise cancellation thanks to the eight microphones, up from six on the XM5 earbuds.

## Sony WF-1000XM6: What's new

### An updated design

![sony case laying flat against red and bluish background](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/05AGLIYBYN3gt692vZMsmtc/images-1.fill.size_2000x1124.v1770849309.jpg)

The XM6s bring a few minor, but important, changes. Credit: Joe Maldonado / Mashable

One of the bigger changes on these earbuds is also one of the more visually apparent. The case loses some of the rounded sides of the XM5 for sharper edges (with rounded ends on either side). The earbuds themselves also take on a new, more oval shape, as compared to the circular design of the XM5s. Sony made this change so the earbud could better fit the inner ear.

I was able to achieve a more flush fit with these earbuds without sacrificing comfort, which I attribute in part to their shape. It's not significantly smaller — Sony says the buds are 11 percent slimmer than the XM5 buds — but less surface area means there's *slightly* more of a learning curve in using the touch controls.

### Better noise cancellation

These earbuds also get a noticeable upgrade in their ANC power. While some parts of the system have remained the same from their predecessor (more on that shortly), the XM6 earbuds come equipped with eight microphones (four are housed in each bud) to the XM5's six. The result is ANC that's truly incredible — so much so that I find it to be some of, if not *the* best, I've ever tried.

On top of that, Sony says the ANC is now so good that even if you wear the buds more loosely in your ear, they still block out the majority of sound.

### Improved sound quality

[Sony's best headphones and earbuds](https://mashable.com/roundup/best-sony-headphones-2025) are known for their stellar sound quality, and the XM6 earbuds are no exception. When listening side-by-side to the XM5 earbuds, it's easy to hear a jump in the depth and clarity of the sound. The newer earbuds evoke a richness and attention to detail, whether you're listening to pop, rock, R&B, classical, or a podcast. (You can learn more about how they [compare to other earbuds in my full review](https://mashable.com/review/sony-wf-1000xm6-earbuds), and a more in-depth comparison to the XM5 earbuds is on its way.)

To power the improved audio features, the XM6 buds have a new processor. They also have a new driver with a high-rigidity dome and notched edges, which provides better clarity and clearer high-frequency audio.

### Clearer call quality

More mics equal better call quality, and the difference is clear in the XM6 earbuds. In addition to the eight microphones, these earbuds use a new bone conduction sensor, two microphones for AI beamforming, and AI noise reduction to make sure your voice comes through as clear as possible on calls.

### The price point

While the XM5 earbuds are technically priced at $329.99, they weren't released at that price. In fact, it wasn't until September 2025 that their price jumped up from its initial list price of $299.99. While not unheard of in the tariff economy, the price point makes slightly more sense on this new and improved model.

For comparison, [Apple's AirPods Pro 3](https://mashable.com/review/apple-airpods-pro-3) were released last year at $249, while the [Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2 earbuds were](https://mashable.com/review/bose-quietcomfort-ultra-earbuds-2nd-gen) released at $299.

## Sony WF-1000XM6: What's the same

![black sony wf-1000xm6 earbuds and case on red background](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/05AGLIYBYN3gt692vZMsmtc/images-4.fill.size_2000x1124.v1770849585.jpg)

Credit: Joe Maldonado / Mashable

In this era of iterative improvements, Sony didn't completely reinvent the XM6 earbuds, so naturally, they have some overlap with the XM5 earbuds. Here's what they have in common:

1. **The same battery life**: Both earbud generations come with eight hours of battery life per charge, with 24 hours in the case.
2. **Noise isolation earbud tips:** Unlike other buds that opt for super smooth silicone ear tips, Sony's noise isolation earbud tips have a more grippy, foam-like feel to help provide the best fit and passive ANC possible. Though parts of the design have changed, Sony hasn't touched the earbud tips between the XM5 and XM6 earbuds.
3. **The same fine print:** Like their predecessor, the XM6 have IPX4 water resistance and multipoint connection with two devices.

args.summary: Sony's new flagship WF-1000XM6 earbuds officially launched on February 12, 2026, priced at $329.99 — a $30 increase over the XM5's launch price of $299.99. The earbuds feature a new QN3e processor, 8 microphones (up from 6), improved active noise cancellation, enhanced sound quality with a new driver, and a redesigned more oval-shaped bud and case. Key specs include 8 hours battery life per charge (24 hours with case), IPX4 water resistance, USB-C and Qi wireless charging, support for SBC/AAC/LDAC/LC3 codecs, and multipoint connection. What remains unchanged from the XM5 is the battery life, noise isolation earbud tips, IPX4 rating, and multipoint connectivity. The reviewer describes the ANC as "some of, if not the best, I've ever tried" and notes the earbuds are available in platinum silver and black at Sony, Amazon, Best Buy, and other retailers.

So, we've been keeping a secret from you guys. Back in January at CES, we actually got our hands on Sony's new flagship earbuds. We just couldn't tell you about them until now. But now, we can finally lift the veil and show you Sony's new WF1000 XM6 flagship earbuds. So, for the past few weeks, we've been running these earbuds through our labs, measuring them, and I've been using them as my daily driver. All to answer a few key questions. Did Sony fix what needed fixing with the XM5s? How do the new XM6 earbuds compare to the competition? And perhaps most importantly, are these new earbuds worth their increased price tag of $330? So, first off, let's talk about some of the most obvious differences between the XM6 and the XM5s, and that's in design. Gone are the glossy egg-shaped earbuds from the XM5. The WF100XM6 now sports a larger pillshaped profile that's way easier to grip thanks to the new matte finish. And thank goodness that glossy coating is gone because those things were slippery as hell and I hated fiddling with them in my ears. The case is about the same width and length as the XM5s, but now stands several millime taller with flat top and bottom surfaces, so it can stand upright on your desk or on a wireless charging pad. The case sure looks bigger, but don't worry, it is still just as pocketable. I could easily slide it into my watch pocket of my jeans without any issue. Right off the bat, I will say that if you are someone who has smaller ears, these earbuds might not be for you. They're noticeably taller in ear than the XM5s and they stick out much further than them as well. They probably stick out too much to be comfortable if you're laying against a pillow or trying to sleep with them or something like that. However, there are some subtle improvements to the fit here. There's a curved indentation on the earbud body that tucks into the cavity of your concha. That's the little B-shaped part of your outer ear. So, it's using your ear's natural anatomy as an anchor point instead of relying purely on the ear tip seal. Now, Sony also claims that this new shape is meant to improve fit consistency across different ear sizes. And in my testing, that actually held up. I was able to get a good seal even if, you know, I was in a rush and having to twist the earbuds in at slightly different angles. So, really, this should benefit those of you who struggle with traditional earbud fits. You know, the kind of people I see on the Sky Train who stick their AirPods in sideways. They can feel a little topheavy in ear, but I was able to wear them for a couple of hours without any fatigue. So, I would say the weight distribution was good enough, at least for my ears. Now, since we're talking about fit, you're probably wondering, did Sony change the ear tips? Well, the answer is no. They come with the exact same four sizes of memory foam ear tips as came with the XM5s. Now, personally, I prefer memory foam to the more common silicone ear tips that come with most earbuds, but if you weren't a fan of the stiffer construction of the ear tips with the XM5s, it's going to be the same deal again here. The larger surface area of the earbuds also makes tap controls a lot more easier to register than on previous Sony models. I found the touch sensors were responsive and accurate throughout my testing. By default, the right earbud handles playback, and the left one manages ambient sound modes, the exact same that was with the XM5, but you can reassign these in the Sony Sound Connect app. Sony has also added optional head gesture controls, so you can do things like accept calls with a nod or reject them with a headshake. These works reliably well, but I typically disabled them because I kept accidentally triggering actions by just, you know, moving my head like a normal person does. The WF-1000XM6 inherits much of the feature set from the recent WH1000XM6 headphones, which means extensive customization through the app. You get things like background music mode, one of my personal favorite additions from the XM6 headphones, by the way. You also get adaptive sound control, speak to chat, and a 10b custom equalizer, which is an improvement over the XM5 sixband EQ. And that just gives you more control over a wider range of frequency bands, each with plus or minus 6 dB of adjustment per band. Now, Sony has also added something called scene-based listening, which promises to select music from your streaming app of choice and match it to your current activity or environment. They've also added spatial sound optimization with head tracking only on Android, however, and spatial sound optimization is basically just the new name for what was formerly referred to as Sony 360 reality audio. However, the caveat here is that neither of these two features were functional during my early access period. So, be sure to check out our written review in the coming days as we will update that with our impressions once they are live. As for connectivity, the XM6 earbuds support Bluetooth 5.3 with SBC, AAC, LDAC, and LC3 for LE audio. Now, that's the same codec lineup as the XM5s. So, if you're on Android, that means you get high-res wireless audio via LDAC. iPhone users, you're stuck with AAC. I mean, what's new? It's Apple. Now, Sony didn't adopt Bluetooth 6, which could be a future proofing concern, especially at this price point. But don't get me wrong. I mean, Bluetooth 5.3 is still perfectly capable for now. It just means that these won't support any exclusive features that may emerge down the line. They still support OraCast for when that finally rolls out, and Bluetooth multipoint is supported, so you can connect to two devices simultaneously. I didn't have any pairing issues either, and switching between my phone and laptop was pretty seamless. I did however experience occasional connection drops while walking around downtown when I didn't prioritize stable connection as a setting within the app. Say if I had something like prioritizing music quality instead. So that was a little annoying to have happen when I didn't have that setting selected, but overall it's not really a dealbreaker. All right, on to battery life. So Sony claims eight hours on a single charge with up to 24 hours total with the case. Now, these are the exact same specs again as with the previous XM5 as well as the previous XM4 earbuds before it. So, yes, Sony has not improved battery life across three generations of earbuds now, but honestly, 8 hours is still the ballpark for all the top competitors nowadays, and that just seems to be a ceiling that hardware is hitting when it comes to wireless earbuds. But to end with a positive note here, in our testing, the WF100XM6 actually lasted 9 hours and 41 minutes, which is higher than Sony's claim. You also still get quick charge with 3 minutes of charging, giving you up to 60 minutes of play time. In reality though, with&c on, I got closer to about 4540 minutes, but that was still more than enough for my daily commute. All right, on to call quality. Now, this was a bit of a sore spot with the previous XM5 earbuds, and I'm happy to report that the Sony WF100XM6 delivers significant improvements in microphone performance. Sony upgraded the microphone system with AI powered beam forming, an improved bone conduction sensor, and AI noise rejection. In quiet environments, I found my voice came through clearly with minimal reverb. Outdoors, the microphones handled wind and ambient noise really well, which was a big improvement over the XM5, which I found those really struggled, especially in windy conditions. On busy streets with a lot of traffic passing by, noise rejection was a little less consistent and occasionally loud vehicles did break through, but my voice clarity still remain much better than when that happened with the XM5 earbuds. In fact, you're actually hearing audio from the XM6 earbuds right now. I've got it recording on my phone and we've got some simulated traffic noise playing off to the side. And if you want to hear how they perform across our full suite of test environments from ideal conditions to office noise, street noise, wind, reverberate spaces, head on over to soundguys.com and check out our full review. So overall, the mics on the XM6 earbuds are much more capable for everyday calls, video conferences, and voice recordings. No big complaints from me here. All right, getting into the stuff all of you guys have been waiting for. How is the active noise cancellation? Well, based on our lab data, the WF-1000XM6 delivers excellent active noise cancellation with an 88% average reduction in loudness across all frequencies, which is an improvement over the XM5's 87%, though not that statistically significant of an improvement overall. It also still trails behind the AirPod Pro 3's 90% average, which is the highest we've ever measured. But even though the average of 88 and 87% might not sound like a difference, and it certainly isn't in terms of averages, there are some noticeable improvements in a few key areas. So, Sony upgraded the hardware with eight microphones now, up from six on the XM5, and this expanded mic gives the earbuds much more data when it comes to analyzing and cancelling outside noise. As you can see in our measurement charts, the most dramatic improvement appears around 100 htz and 2 kohertz, where the WF100XM6 attenuates over 40 dB and 50 dB, respectively. Now, that means low-end noise like air conditioners and incidental sounds like keyboard clatter are nearly completely silenced. However, the ANC is less effective in that 400 to 2 kHz mid-range, so you may still hear some voices and office chatter breaking through. I tested these pretty extensively on buses and busy downtown streets, and the earbuds handled everything pretty admirably. A large part of that is due to the upgraded processor that also now features a new adaptive ANC optimizer, which basically analyzes external noise and wearing conditions in real time. So that means these earbuds can adapt quickly, say when moving from a quiet office out onto a noisy subway platform. One quirk, however, though, is that if you do manually toggle ambient mode with a tap of a finger while this feature is enabled, the earbuds will sometimes protest and revert back to&C, which can be a little bit annoying. You know, it's not a dealbreaker, but I don't like having to fight with my earbuds. like when I'm manually trying to activate something, that should override whatever settings the app were trying to fight me on. All right, now perhaps the most important question, how do these earbuds sound? In one sentence, these are Sony's best sounding earbuds to date. The stock tuning is likely to please most people without any major gripes. I was pretty impressed with how clean and detailed most music sounds. Listening to some glam rock stuff like Foxy Shazam. I could easily separate instruments and vocals even in dense mixes with group harmonies and horns. Vocals in particular sounded especially clear and natural, and I was able to hear details from things like symbols and tambourines that I don't always catch. Switching over to some psychedelic rock like Tame and Pala, the fuzzy bass guitar riffs came through with excellent detail. I could really hear the character of the distortion without ever losing any bass precision. However, and this is one caveat, the bass did sound a bit too loud only when I had A&C enabled. I actually preferred listening with ANC disabled for a more balanced mix. Sometimes string instruments had a bit of a boxy quality. You know, that kind of hollow sound almost as if they were being played inside a small box. But honestly, that's a bit of a nitpick and something I was easily able to address within the custom equalizer. Looking at our charts, the WF-1000 XM6's frequency response tracks fairly closely to our house curve, even with ANC enabled. Now, there's a modest amount of overemphasis through the bass and lower mids, you know, from 20 to 400 hertz, which can cause bass guitars, kick drums, and electronic music to sound a bit louder than you might prefer. The upper mids remain well represented with only minor deviations that shouldn't affect speech or instrument clarity. There is also some overemphasis in the treble region around 6 kHz where things like symbol shimmer, vocal breiness, and a lot of high frequency details live. Now, these elements can sound louder, creating the impression of added clarity, although some listeners may find it slightly sharp or fatiguing for extended listening. Now, here's something a little bit odd, which you might have already guessed, which is that the frequency response does change when you disable active noise cancellation. As you can see from the charts, with ANC turned off, the WF1000XM6 exhibits less emphasis in the bass and mid-range, tracking much closer to our house curve. So, if you find the default bass emphasis to be too much, you may actually prefer listening with A&C disabled. Though, you'll obviously lose the noise cancellation benefits, which is a bit of a bummer. Now, charts are one thing, but how would a few hundred listeners rate the sound of the XM6 earbuds out of five? Well, according to the head acoustics MDAX testing, our virtual panel of listeners would rate the Sony WF1000XM6 an overall score of 4.8 on a scale of 1 to5. Compared to other earbuds we've tested, that is a very high score. And that high score owes a lot to Sony's tuning and strong ability to maintain a convincing illusion of 3D space with a stereo image. Notably, I also want to give Sony props for improving the distortion handling compared to the previous WF-1000XM5. If I had to guess, the less distortion there is likely due to the new drivers here, which do now feature notches in the edge section. So, wrapping it all up, should you rush out and drop 330 bucks on the new Sony WF1000XM6? Well, it depends. If you already own the previous WF1000XM5, the improvements here probably aren't enough to justify the upgrade. The fit is better, the sound is marginally improved, the ANC is modestly better, and the microphones are significantly better, but battery life and codecs and everything else remains identical and you're pretty much paying $30 more for the privilege. However, if you are on the XM4 or something older or maybe switching from another brand entirely, I do think the WF1000XM6 delivers a flagship performance across the board. Sony focused on getting the important things right and perhaps a known surprise, they succeeded. So, yes, the Sony WX1000XM6 are excellent earbuds. I can't take that away from them. But just like the WH1000XM6 headphones, nothing is ever perfect. They fix mistakes, refined the formula, and delivered a strong flagship product. So, whether or not that's enough for you will depend on what you're upgrading from, and what you value most in your earbuds. If you want to see how Sony's tackling the overyear headphone market, then check out our review of the WH100 XM6 headphones right over there. And be sure to subscribe to the channel so you don't miss our in-depth comparisons for how these earbuds stack up against the top competitors like the AirPods Pro 3.

# Sony WF-1000XM6 Review Summary

## Overview
The Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds were released in February 2026 (review posted Feb 12, 2026) with a price tag of $330. SoundGuys conducted lab testing and real-world usage to evaluate Sony's claims of "best noise cancellation," "higher call quality," "enhanced comfort," and "most ideal sound."

## Design & Fit
- Redesigned from glossy egg-shape (XM5) to larger pill-shaped matte finish, easier to grip
- Case is slightly taller with flat top/bottom, can stand upright, metal hinge for durability
- Noticeably larger than XM5s; may not suit smaller ears; stick out too much for sleeping
- Curved indentation uses ear's natural anatomy (concha) as anchor point for better fit consistency
- Same memory foam ear tips (4 sizes) as XM5

## Controls & Features
- Touch sensors responsive; tap controls easier to register
- Optional head gesture controls (nod to accept calls, shake to reject) but prone to accidental triggers
- Sony Sound Connect app with: 10-band custom EQ (up from 6-band), background music mode, adaptive sound control, speak-to-chat, scene-based listening, spatial sound optimization with head tracking (Android only)
- Some features were not functional during early access period

## Connectivity
- Bluetooth 5.3 (not Bluetooth 6 — potential future-proofing concern)
- Codecs: SBC, AAC, LDAC, LC3 for LE audio
- Bluetooth multipoint (2 devices simultaneously)
- Occasional connection drops when prioritizing music quality over stable connection

## Battery Life
- Claimed: 8 hours (single charge), 24 hours total (with case)
- Lab tested: 9 hours 41 minutes (exceeds claim)
- Quick charge: 3 minutes = ~45-60 minutes play time
- Battery life unchanged across three generations (XM4, XM5, XM6)

## Microphone/Call Quality (Significant improvement)
- Upgraded system: AI-powered beamforming, improved bone conduction sensor, AI noise rejection
- Clear voice in quiet environments; handles wind and ambient noise well outdoors
- Still occasional issues with loud vehicles breaking through on busy streets
- Overall "much more capable for everyday calls, video conferences, and voice recordings"

## Active Noise Cancellation
- 88% average reduction in loudness (vs. XM5's 87%, AirPods Pro 3's 90% — highest ever measured)
- 8 microphones (up from 6 on XM5)
- Dramatic improvements around 100 Hz and 2 kHz (40-50 dB attenuation)
- New adaptive ANC optimizer for real-time adaptation
- Quirk: manual ambient mode toggle sometimes overridden by ANC

## Sound Quality
- Described as "Sony's best sounding earbuds to date"
- Stock tuning: clean, detailed, clear vocals, good instrument separation
- Bass slightly too loud with ANC enabled; more balanced with ANC off
- Frequency response tracks close to house curve with ANC enabled
- Bass/lower mids slightly overemphasized (20-400 Hz)
- Treble overemphasis around 6 kHz (may cause listener fatigue)
- Distortion handling improved (likely due to new drivers with notches in edge section)
- MDAQS score: 4.8/5 (very high)

## Verdict
- **For XM5 owners**: Improvements not enough to justify $330 upgrade (fit, sound, ANC marginally better; mics significantly better; battery/codecs identical)
- **For XM4 owners or switching brands**: "Flagship performance across the board" — recommended
- Sony "fixed mistakes, refined the formula, and delivered a strong flagship product"

Apple’s official site lists the AirPods Pro 3 at $249 with no discount, no promotion, and no indication that will change anytime soon. Amazon is doing things differently: the AirPods Pro 3 are down to [$189, off their $249 list price and at their all-time low on Amazon since launch](https://shop.gizmodo.com/go/4010/). No Prime membership required.

[See at Amazon](https://shop.gizmodo.com/go/4010/)

## 2x better ANC, heart rate sensing, Live Translation

The AirPods Pro 3 deliver active noise cancellation that Apple claims removes up to twice as much unwanted noise as the AirPods Pro 2, which was already the benchmark for ANC in the earbuds category. The acoustic architecture was rebuilt from the ground up, with a new driver and amplifier system that delivers noticeably more bass depth and vocal clarity than the previous generation. Personalized Spatial Audio maps your ear geometry and adjusts the three-dimensional soundstage to your specific anatomy, and next-generation Adaptive EQ continuously fine-tunes the frequency response based on how the earbuds sit in your ear at any given moment.

Heart rate sensing is the feature addition that most meaningfully separates the Pro 3 from every previous AirPods generation. The earbuds track heart rate and calories burned across more than 50 workout types, feeding data to the Move ring and the new Workout Buddy feature on iPhone via Apple Intelligence. Live Translation handles real-time speech translation across language barriers directly through the earbuds, without requiring a phone to be held up or an app to be opened manually.

## Hearing Aid feature, hearing test, Hearing Protection

The Hearing Aid feature introduced on the AirPods Pro 2 returns on the Pro 3 with automatic Conversation Boost, which amplifies nearby speech in real time for users with mild to moderate hearing loss. A hearing test can be taken at home through the Health app, and the results are used to personalize the Hearing Aid output to the specific frequency profile of your hearing. Active Hearing Protection monitors environmental noise levels and automatically reduces exposure when sound exceeds safe thresholds, which is a passive safety feature that runs in the background without requiring manual activation.

Battery life runs to 8 hours with Active Noise Cancellation enabled, or up to 10 hours in Transparency and Hearing Aid mode. Five ear tip sizes cover a wider range of ear geometries than the four sizes offered on the Pro 2, and the all-new tip design provides a more secure seal that improves both passive isolation and bass response. The case charges via USB-C and supports Qi wireless charging.

Ten thousand reviews averaging 4.5 stars in the time since launch is a strong early signal for a product at this price point, and the complaints that appear are minor software quibbles rather than hardware concerns. At $189, the AirPods Pro 3 are $60 below what Apple charges today on its own storefront, on a product that Apple has never discounted directly. That gap is unlikely to close until Apple decides to formally acknowledge a price reduction, which based on its track record is not imminent.

args.summary:
The SoundGuys review of the Beats Studio Pro (posted Nov 10, 2024) evaluates the headphones well after their initial release. The reviewer finds the Beats Studio Pro NOT worth their $349 retail price but recommends buying them if available on sale (commonly found around $170 during Prime Day, Black Friday, and other sales).

**Pros:**
1. **Sound Quality (4.8/5 MDAQS score):** The headphones have moved away from Beats' traditionally bass-heavy signature. Frequency response measurements closely align with SoundGuys' preference curve, with a slight sub-bass boost (adds rumble to kick drums) and a treble emphasis between 5-10kHz (enhances reverb/immersion but may make cymbals and hi-hats sound shrill to some).
2. **Active Noise Cancellation:** Reduces outside noise by an average of 79% (good, but less than Sony WH-1000XM5); effective enough to mute cars and subway screeching.
3. **Cross-Platform Compatibility:** Works well on both iOS and Android. Android users can download the Beats app for firmware updates and customizing controls. iOS users get additional features like spatial audio and audio sharing.

**Cons:**
1. **Design/Comfort Issues:** Loud clicky buttons on the left ear cup; tight clamping force becomes uncomfortable after a few hours; ear cups are small and barely accommodate average-sized ears. Recommended to try in-store before buying.
2. **Weird EQ Limitation:** The three EQ presets can only be used when connected via USB-C cable, not over Bluetooth.
3. **Price:** $349 retail is too high given better alternatives exist (Sony WH-1000XM5, Bose QuietComfort).

**Verdict:** Buy only on sale (around $170). At sale price, they offer good value as mid-tier headphones with decent ANC, good sound quality, and cross-platform compatibility.

Anker Soundcore makes some of the [best budget earbuds](https://www.soundguys.com/best-wireless-earbuds-under-200-73754/) we’ve ever tested. The [Liberty 4](https://www.soundguys.com/anker-soundcore-liberty-4-nc-review-100100/) lineup set a high bar, and the standard [Liberty 5](https://www.soundguys.com/anker-soundcore-liberty-5-review-137445/) earbuds didn’t quite clear it. But now, the Liberty 5 Pro is finally here with a completely rethought design, a smarter case, and a lot more ambition. If you want serious features and performance without serious spending, these might be exactly what you’ve been waiting for.

**About this Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro review:** We tested the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro over a period of one week. The company provided the unit for this review.

This article was published on May 21, 2026, and this is the first version of the article. Updates will follow as the market changes.



## What’s it like to use the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro?

The Liberty 5 Pro are comfortable, well-designed earbuds with a useful Smart Screen case and more features than you’d expect at this price.

### Design

The conha fins keep the large earbuds stable.

The Liberty 5 Pros ditch the stem design that Anker often uses in favor of a new, slightly curved oval shape. I would say it’s closer in profile to the Bose QuietComfort Earbuds than anything in Soundcore’s previous lineup. Although they are larger than before, they are fairly comfortable.

I usually prefer the natural anchor that a stem design creates by sitting between the tragus and antitragus, but even though the Liberty 5 Pro loses that, they remain stable thanks to the fin at the top of the earbud that tucks into the concha. If fins aren’t your thing or don’t fit your ear shape, Anker includes two flush plastic pieces you can snap in instead, so the earbuds sit smoothly against your ears. You also get five sizes of ear tips, which is a fairly generous offering at this price point, to help get a good seal.

I tried these at the gym and had no problem with stability during my workout. They carry an IP55 rating, meaning they’re water- and dust-resistant, offering solid protection from sweat. Controls are handled via swipe gestures on the earbud surface, primarily up or down to adjust volume by default. You can also assign single-, double-, and triple-tap functions within the app.

The charging case also features a narrow touchscreen along the front, displays battery levels at a glance, and lets you swipe left or right to cycle through sound modes without touching your phone. The lid slides open rather than flipping, which is nice, and the charging port sits on the back. It’s compact enough, but it can be a bit big in the pocket.

### Features

The Soundcore app offers EQ presets and audio customization options.

The Soundcore app opens up plenty of features for the Liberty 5 Pros. The first one I recommend starting with is HearID, a listening test that builds a personalized EQ profile based on your hearing. From there, there’s also a standard eight-band custom equalizer to tweak things further, along with four EQ presets: Powerful Bass, Clear Vocals, Calm and Soothing, and Balanced.

On top of that, the app gives you access to Dolby Audio, which adds a spatial sound effect to music and supports head tracking, where the sound field shifts as you move your head. It’s the same kind of feature you’d find on AirPods, and I found the results varied by genre.

Of course, you also now have Anka, Soundcore’s new built-in AI assistant. Activated by saying “Hey Anka,” it can answer questions, give you weather updates, and handle basic playback commands — all hands-free. More practically useful is the real-time translation feature, which continuously translates spoken languages through the earbuds with minimal lag, and a face-to-face translation mode for back-and-forth conversations. These are all pretty useful features you don’t typically find at this price.

Powering the AI features is Anker’s new Thus chip, designed specifically for on-device AI processing in small, battery-constrained devices like earbuds. The practical upshot is that features like Anka and Clear Calls — Soundcore’s AI-based environmental noise cancelation for phone calls — run locally on the earbuds rather than relying on a cloud connection, and do so without the battery drain you might expect.



## How does the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro connect?

The Liberty 5 Pros use Bluetooth 6.1 with support for SBC, AAC, and [LDAC](https://www.soundguys.com/ldac-ultimate-bluetooth-guide-20026/) for higher-resolution wireless audio on compatible Android devices. The earbuds also support Google Fast Pair for instant pairing on Android. If you’re on an iPhone, you’ll top out at AAC.

Multipoint is enabled by default, letting you stay connected to up to three devices at once, which is pretty handy if you’re switching between a phone, tablet, and laptop throughout the day. One caveat, however, is that LDAC is unavailable when connected to three devices, so you’ll need to drop down to two if audio quality is the priority.



## How long does the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro’s battery last?

The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro case features a front-facing display for monitoring battery levels.

Soundcore rates the Liberty 5 Pros at up to 12 hours of playback with ANC off, or 6.5 hours with ANC on. By comparison, the standard Liberty 5 lasted 8 hours with ANC on, so there’s a trade-off for the extra features. Combined with the charging case, you’re looking at up to 50 hours total with ANC off, or 28 hours with ANC on. A five-minute charge delivers up to four hours of playback. The case charges via USB-C or Qi wireless charging.



## How well do the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro cancel noise?

The Liberty 5 Pro offers five levels of ANC strength adjustable in the app, plus an Adaptive mode that automatically tunes cancellation to your environment. At full blast, and with [a good seal](https://www.soundguys.com/what-is-isolation-12506/), the earbuds attenuate the perceived loudness of outside noise by an average of nearly 84%, which is pretty impressive for earbuds at this price. I found they effectively blocked out the constant low-frequency drone of my bus ride to work.

### How good is the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Transparency mode?

The Liberty 5 Pros include a transparency mode accessible from the earbuds, the app, or the Smart Screen on the case. There’s also a feature called Easy Chat, which automatically switches to transparency and lowers your music volume when it detects you’re speaking, then returns to your previous ANC level and volume about five seconds after you stop talking. I found it pretty useful for quick conversations, like ordering a coffee, without having to pull out my phone or tap my earbuds.



## How do the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro sound?

Like many Anker Soundcore earbuds and headphones, the Liberty 5 Pro has strong bass overemphasis by default. Thankfully, the custom EQ can tame it if that’s not your thing, and most listeners will find they sound enjoyable straight out of the box.

### Reviewer’s notes

*Editor’s note: this review uses a hover-enabled glossary to describe sound quality based on a consensus vocabulary. You can read about it*[***here***](https://www.soundguys.com/headphone-reviews-problems-67837/)*.*



## Can you use the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro for phone calls?

The Liberty 5 Pros use an onboard 8-microphone array along with 2 bone-conduction sensors to capture your voice and filter out background noise. In ideal conditions, call clarity is pretty good. Voices come through clearly, though I did notice the occasional pop or crackle.

If you’re regularly taking calls in noisy environments, it’s worth enabling Clear Calls in the Soundcore app. It’s designed to do a more thorough job of isolating your voice than standard algorithms, though enabling it alongside other features like LDAC or voice control will draw on the battery more quickly.

Noise rejection is decent overall. Background noise is noticeably quieter rather than completely eliminated, and there can be a slight delay before the noise cancelation kicks in. args.summary:
This is a product review of the Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro wireless earbuds published on May 21, 2026, by SoundGuys. The earbuds are priced at $169.99 and received an overall rating of 8.1/10 from SoundGuys and 7.9/10 from users. They are positioned as one of the best value wireless earbuds under $200.

Key features and specifications:
- IP55 water and dust resistance rating
- Bluetooth 6.1 with support for SBC, AAC, and LDAC codecs
- Multipoint connection for up to 3 devices simultaneously
- Battery life: Up to 12 hours (ANC off) / 6.5 hours (ANC on); total with case up to 50 hours (ANC off) / 28 hours (ANC on); 5-minute quick charge provides 4 hours of playback
- USB-C and Qi wireless charging case with a front-facing touchscreen display
- 8-microphone array with 2 bone-conduction sensors for calls
- Features: HearID personalized EQ, Dolby Audio with spatial sound and head tracking, "Anka" AI assistant, real-time language translation, Adaptive ANC with 5 levels, transparency mode with Easy Chat (auto-switches to transparency when speaking)
- Powered by Anker's new Thus chip for on-device AI processing

Design changes from previous models: Ditch stem design for curved oval shape (similar to Bose QuietComfort Earbuds), includes concha fins for stability with alternative flush plastic pieces, comes with 5 sizes of ear tips.

Pros: Price, ANC, features, comfort, Bluetooth 6.1 with LDAC
Cons: Bass-heavy default tuning, ANC effects sound

The review notes the default sound profile has strong bass overemphasis but can be tamed via custom EQ. ANC attenuates perceived loudness by nearly 84%. Call quality is decent with good noise rejection, though wind conditions introduce a reverberant quality.

Alternatives mentioned: Sony WF-C710N ($119.99) for better ANC at lower price, Creative Aurvana Ace 3 ($149.99) for better sound quality.

# Soundcore announces 2 earbuds that lean into AI for better call quality and smart feature performance

The earbuds are the first Soundcore products to feature the new Anker THUS AI chip.

By

[Bethany Allard](/author/bethanyallard)

![two pairs of soundcore earbuds on wooden tabletop](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/00FKTsDbtUX6oGzuVWQOVXF/hero-image.fill.size_1248x702.v1779398231.jpg)

Meet the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max and 5 Pro.  Credit: Bethany Allard / Mashable

## Table of Contents

Soundcore announced two new pairs of earbuds during its Anker Day event on May 21: the [Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro](https://zdcs.link/z64rP7?pageview_type=Standard&template=article&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=Soundcore%20Liberty%205%20Pro&object_type=article&object_uuid=00FKTsDbtUX6oGzuVWQOVXF&short_url=z64rP7&u=https%3A%2F%2Fmashable.com%2Farticle-route-prefix%2Ftech%2Fsoundcore-liberty-5-pro-and-pro-max-launch-price-first-impressions "(opens in a new window)") and [Liberty 5 Pro Max](https://zdcs.link/a074Ve?pageview_type=Standard&template=article&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=Liberty%205%20Pro%20Max&object_type=article&object_uuid=00FKTsDbtUX6oGzuVWQOVXF&short_url=a074Ve&u=https%3A%2F%2Fmashable.com%2Farticle-route-prefix%2Ftech%2Fsoundcore-liberty-5-pro-and-pro-max-launch-price-first-impressions "(opens in a new window)").

The earbuds are the first Soundcore products to feature the new THUS AI chip, designed to boost the performance of the earbuds' microphone for call quality, voice activation, and smart features like live translation and AI note-taking. Spoiler alert: the mic performance is no joke on these earbuds.

SEE ALSO:  [The 11 best wireless earbuds we've ever tested](/roundup/best-wireless-earbuds-tested)

Both the Liberty 5 Pro and Liberty 5 Pro Max are available as of May 21. I've spent a few days trying out both pairs of earbuds — below you'll find my first impressions, the specs, price, and everything else you need to know about Soundcore's latest audio release.

---

 **You May Also Like** 

---

---

## Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro: Specs and price

The Liberty 5 Pro is available for $169.99 and comes with the following feature set:

![blue soundcore liberty 5 pro case and earbuds on green table](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/00FKTsDbtUX6oGzuVWQOVXF/images-4.fill.size_2000x1125.v1779398232.jpg)

The Liberty 5 Pro come with a small on-case display. Credit: Bethany Allard / Mashable

* **Battery:** 6.5 hours with ANC (28 hours with charging case), 12 hours without ANC (50 hours with charging case)
* **Active noise cancellation:** Yes, adaptive and five levels of manually adjustable ANC
* **Microphones:** 8 microphones, plus two bone conduction sensors
* **Connection:** Bluetooth 6.1
* **Multipoint:** Yes, up to three devices simultaneously
* **IP rating:** IP55
* **Ear tips:** Five sizes, from XXS to L
* **Ear fins:** Three sizes
* **Colors:** Blue, white, black, and pink

## Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro: First impressions

I haven't had the chance to test the full range of the Liberty 5 Pro features just yet, but as Soundcore emphasizes the "whisper clear" calls these buds are capable of, I made sure to get in some testing of the microphone, along with the usual suspects of the sound quality (rich and well-varied, from my initial listens) and active noise cancellation.

### Mic quality is superb

Call quality may seem like a weird feature to brag about, but if you've used earbuds with a crappy microphone, you know how annoying it can be to have to disconnect your earbuds every time you need to take a call.

My first test for these earbuds was an informal one. While FaceTiming a friend and wearing these earbuds, another friend in the room with me leaned into the frame of my phone's camera to say hello. My friend on the other end of the call happened to be looking away — she had no clue the other person in the room with me had spoken at all. Meanwhile, she could hear me without any issue. Whisper clear indeed. I've also been able to hold full conversations with ease while other people are watching TV and chatting in the same room, while the person on the other side of the call has been none the wiser. All this to say, the early results are very promising.

So is it really just a matter of matching up a full set of microphones with an AI chip? Not exactly. Soundcore goes the extra mile, adding two bone conduction sensors to detect vibrations in your skull and ensure that only your voice is picked up, even in noisier environments.

### The noise cancellation is no joke either

I nearly jumped out of my skin when someone approached me to say good morning while I was listening to music on these earbuds at about 40 percent volume. Apparently, they'd been trying to get my attention for a good 30 seconds. So that's another informal test, passed.

On a more technical note, these earbuds have eight microphones that work together with the THUS chip to provide the best possible noise cancellation. The result is impressive, especially considering their $169.99 price point. While I look forward to testing them out and about in the world more, as far as my home office (and simply existing in a house where seven other people live), these earbuds are more than getting the job done so far.

### Comfortable and stable

The ear fin/ear tip combo on these earbuds reminds me a lot of the [Bose QuietComfort earbuds series](https://mashable.com/roundup/best-bose-headphones-earbuds). Whenever I'm positively comparing the wear of earbuds to the QC series, that's a very, very good thing, considering the Bose buds are the most comfortable I've tested.

The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max is available for $229.99, with the following feature set:

The Liberty 5 Pro Max comes with a larger display on the case and the ability to record meetings for AI note-taking.  Credit: Bethany Allard / Mashable

* **Battery:** 6.5 hours with ANC (28 hours with charging case), 12 hours without ANC (50 hours with charging case)
* **Active noise cancellation:** Yes, adaptive and five levels of manually adjustable ANC
* **Microphones:** 8 microphones, plus two bone conduction sensors
* **Connection:** Bluetooth 6.1
* **Multipoint:** Yes, up to three devices simultaneously
* **IP rating:** IP55
* **Ear tips:** Five sizes, from XXS to L
* **Ear fins:** Three sizes
* **Colors:** Titanium-gold and black

## Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max: First impressions

The Liberty 5 Pro Max earbuds have many of the same features as the 5 Pro, including the same tech for powering noise cancellation, sound quality, and the microphones. They also feature the same earbud shape. There is *one* notable difference, though, which we'll get into below:

### The mic impresses on the Pro Max buds, too

The Pro Max earbuds use the same 10-sensor matrix (the microphones and bone conduction sensors) as the 5 Pro earbuds, so it's no surprise that, in combination with the AI chipset, these earbuds also sounded incredible on calls and did a reliable job at blocking out background noise.

Living in a house with seven other people means that if I'm not at my desk (and even then), there's at least a 50 percent chance that I'll take a call while someone else is having a conversation around me. For the times that's happened so far, not once did the people on the other side of the call hear the background noise from my end. My next tests will involve taking these earbuds out into the world (for even louder and more distracting environments).

### A larger display on the earbuds case

![liberty 5 pro max case with anc screen on display](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/00FKTsDbtUX6oGzuVWQOVXF/images-5.fill.size_2000x1125.v1779398232.jpg)

The entire top of the case acts as a display for customizing features on the earbuds. Credit: Bethany Allard / Mashable

The 5 Pro Max has an even bigger touchscreen on the charging case than the 5 Pro, which takes up the entire top of the case. The 1.78-inch AMOLED display allows you to access many of the same features as the smaller 5 Pro case, plus the AI note-taking feature, which uses the case to record the conversation.

### AI note-taking feature isn't anything to scoff at either

As a journalist, I'm especially into any easy way to record interviews or conversations, and Soundcore seeks to do just that with its AI note-taker. Basically, it works as the case records the conversation, meeting, talk — whatever you're trying to get down. Then, it transfers the file to the companion app, and, at your request, can generate a transcript and summary with identified speakers.

During the recording, a tap of the flag button creates markers in the recording that become highlighted in the transcription. Before creating the transcription, you can also select the recording type (discussion, presentation, etc.), so the AI can choose the best format for the information.

So far, I could see this being an incredibly useful tool, but I'm also interested to see the limitations (it looks like a Pro version for more transcription minutes is available) and how it compares to Apple's built-in voice memo feature.

### Noise cancellation and sound quality

In my testing so far, the noise cancellation and sound quality are basically indistinguishable from the 5 Pro earbuds, which is to say they both sound really good and do a great job of blocking out sound.

One hiccup I noticed while testing the adaptive ANC on the 5 Pro Max buds was a soft clicking sound in the left earbud — it was almost not detectable while audio was playing, but without music, it was definitely present. It could've just been a glitch that a software update will fix, so I'll be keeping my eye on it as I head further into my testing period.

args.summary:
Soundcore announced two new earbuds — the Liberty 5 Pro ($169.99) and Liberty 5 Pro Max ($229.99) — during its Anker Day event on May 21. Both are the first Soundcore products to feature the new THUS AI chip, designed to enhance microphone performance for call quality, voice activation, and smart features like live translation and AI note-taking.

**Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro ($169.99):**
- Battery: 6.5 hours with ANC (28 hours with case), 12 hours without ANC (50 hours with case)
- 8 microphones + 2 bone conduction sensors, adaptive ANC with 5 manual levels, Bluetooth 6.1, multipoint up to 3 devices, IP55 rating
- Comes with 5 ear tip sizes (XXS to L) and 3 ear fin sizes
- Colors: blue, white, black, pink
- Charging case has a 0.96-inch mini touchscreen for ANC, EQ, spatial audio, and Bluetooth settings
- Early impressions: excellent mic quality (isolates voice in noisy environments), impressive ANC for the price point, comfortable fit (compared favorably to Bose QuietComfort series)

**Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max ($229.99):**
- Same specs as 5 Pro for battery, ANC, microphones, connection, IP rating
- Available in titanium-gold and black
- Larger 1.78-inch AMOLED touchscreen covering the entire top of the case
- Exclusive AI note-taking feature: the case records conversations/meetings, transfers to the companion app, and generates transcripts and summaries with identified speakers. Includes flag markers for important moments.
- Early impressions: same excellent mic quality and ANC as the 5 Pro; a minor clicking sound was noted in the left earbud during adaptive ANC testing (possibly a software glitch)

Both models are available from Amazon, Soundcore, and Best Buy as of May 21.

## soundcore Liberty 5 Pro / Liberty 5 Pro Max Product Page Summary

This is the official product page for soundcore's Liberty 5 Pro and Liberty 5 Pro Max true wireless earbuds, marketed as "The World's Clearest Earbuds for Calls."

### Key Product Highlights

**World Record Certification**: The Liberty 5 Pro was certified by Guinness World Records in April 2026 for the "Highest speech quality score (G-MOS) for TWS earbuds (objective test)." The Pro Max features identical earbud units with the same call performance.

**Core Technology - ANKER Thus™ AI Chip**: Powered by the world's first neural-net compute-in-memory AI audio chip, delivering 150× computing power compared to the previous flagship earbud chip.

### Key Features

[music] Now, the case does store all the recordings on board until you're back in range of your phone, at which point it automatically transfers everything over, and you can have the recordings deleted from the case. So, overall, I would say that if you are a busy working professional who finds yourself in a lot of meetings or interviews, and you just want to offload all the note-taking to AI, then yeah, this feature could save you a lot of time. That does mean things like cymbals and hi-hats can sound quieter than I'm used to, and at times the overall sound feels slightly more closed in, you know, almost as if sounds are coming from inside my head rather than all around me. # Sony's big oops! ULT Wear Full Review
## Erin Lawrence
