### Transcript:
Sony is making a huge mistake with these headphones and they probably don't even realize it. Or maybe they do. Sony ULT Wear have only been around since 2024 and they're packed with flagship-level features like noise canceling, ambient mode, touch controls, and auto pause. So, what's the catch? I'm Aaron from TechGagetsInternational and I've reviewed probably almost a hundred pairs of headphones. And by the way, if you want to receive my free seven-page headphone and earbud buying guide, hit me with an email right here and put headphone buying guide into the subject line. Now, in this review, I'm going to talk about what makes these headphones special, how they sound, what special features they have, and their puzzling price point. Let's dive into it so you can see what I mean about feeling like there's a catch and the big mistake that I think Sony is making with these. Let's unbox and you can see you're getting a hard fabric-wrapped zippered case. Also in the box is a 3.5 mm audio cable and a USB-A to C charging cable. The headphones are entirely plastic, which at first glance leaves me thinking they're going to be incredibly cheap-feeling. But getting hands-on, I can see the headband has lots of padding on the top with a delightfully zippy adjustable headband that actually feels pretty durable and substantial. And surprisingly, these headphones don't have that cheap hollow-sounding knock to them that a lot of lower-quality over-ear headphones do. There's plenty of thick cushioning and padding on each ear cup, too. And despite the chunky and substantial overall look, these headphones are pretty light at just 255 g. Popping them on my head, they actually feel incredibly well-balanced with a strong but not overwhelming clamping force. The ear cups fit around my ears really well and those cushiony pads actually provide a surprising amount of passive noise isolation, which is a nice perk because the headphones also have noise cancellation, which we'll get to. All the buttons are on the left ear cup. There's power, a button labeled NC/AMB, which will toggle between noise cancellation and ambient mode. And then there is the ULT button, which I'll also get to in a sec. Two ports round out the controls here. There's an aux jack for wired listening and a USB-C charging port. Now, while you wouldn't know it, the right ear cup is a touch pad. Swipe up or down to adjust volume or forward and back for track control. Double tapping the ear cup triggers play or pause. Setup is easy. You'll power these headphones on with a push and hold, and the first time you use them, they should automatically be in pairing mode. Open up your phone's Bluetooth menu and tap to connect. You can also download the Sony Sound Connect app, which is formerly called the Headphones Connect app, and use that to set it up. But either way, you want the app because it'll give you access to a bunch of settings, including toggling between noise cancellation and ambient, adjusting EQ, and connecting to multiple devices, plus a few other things like viewing detailed battery life. Sound quality is usually the key driver in any decision about buying headphones. So, you'll be glad to hear that the audio here is shockingly great. To my ear, these headphones easily stand shoulder to shoulder with some of the top-tier headphones like the WH-1000XM line from Sony, also Bose's QC headphones. And these are shockingly close in quality even to Apple AirPods Max and Dyson Zone Airstream. Given the more budget-friendly price tag of these, I actually extended my sound testing because I wanted to make sure these sounded as good as I thought they did. Where I don't usually do side-by-side comparisons to competitor headphones, here I did try them out against the AirPods Max and Bose QC Ultra second generation just to see if I was losing my mind. Switching back and forth, it was obvious to me how close the sound profiles are and how similar the quality of the Sony ULTs is to other high-end competitors. Now, each of the layers of music is really detectable, while at the same time blending together naturally and beautifully. The bass without any ULT boosting sounds quite good and pleasantly resonant. The highs sail across the top of the sound profile delicately while the vocals are clear and natural and there is no hiss, hum, buzz, or distortion in these. And even tapping on the touchpad on the outside of the ear cup here doesn't echo inside the ear cups and ruin that sound profile with any cheap hollow sounding knocking which by the way is quite common in cheaper plastic builds. In short, these are absolutely fantastic sounding headphones. One key defining feature of the wear headphones is the ULT button on the left ear cup. Unless you've done some reading, you'll have no idea what this button is designed to do and what the ULT name on it is supposed to be about. So, it's a good thing I'm here to translate. Now, pressing the ULT button will activate what Sony unhelpfully calls ULT power sound which it says is designed to up the bass. Now, there are two levels of added bass or you can leave it off. Now, surprisingly, this button does add a lot of bass to the sound and as it turned out almost too much for me at its highest setting and that is saying a lot because I like my bass. Now, the ULT button definitely adds a lot more thump and resonant boom and I actually found my preference was for the lowest level of extra bass. Switching modes, by the way, will quiet the music for a second while it makes the change, but otherwise, the effect is immediately noticeable. Sony ULT wear headphones use the same V1 chip as the Sony XM models which powers the headphones noise cancellation and ambient audio features. When I test out noise cancellation or ambient mode, I first like to try it without any music playing inside the headphones just so I can get a sense of how hard those features are working. I am pretty impressed to say here that the ULT wear performed extremely well at this task and blocked out what felt like 80 to 90% of all the noise around me. Now, while I never reviewed the Sony WH-1000XM6, it is worth pointing out that the ULT Wear here features four built-in microphones, while the XM6 has 12 for better noise canceling performance. But, if I'm getting this level of noise cancellation with just four built-in microphones here, maybe I should get on my horse and review those 1000XM6s, because could it really be even that much better? Now, if you do want to see a review of the 1000XM6, or even a comparison head-to-head, let me know in the comments. I also want to say that ambient mode, which is the ULT Wear's transparency mode, works better and sounds more natural compared to the Sony XM4s I reviewed back in the day. With a lot of cheaper headphones, ambient mode can sound extremely hollow and unnatural, and come with quite a hiss, but here, it just sounded like I wasn't wearing any headphones at all. Very impressive. With the Sony Sound Connect app, you can also fine-tune how much ambient sound you'll get passed through to your ears. A slider bar in the app lets you let in more or less sound, and you can toggle on what's called voice pass-through, which will filter voices into you while suppressing ambient noise. I love this feature because it means if someone next to me is trying to talk to me, I can hear them clearly while filtering out things like the dishwasher running or traffic or machinery noise. Sony ULT Wear inherits the adaptive sound control feature of the Sony XM line as well, which you can toggle on to automatically set the mode to either noise canceling or ambient mode, depending on the activity it detects you doing. How it works is that it can detect movement and ambient noise. So, if you're just sitting at your desk, it'll engage noise cancellation, where if you're jogging or walking outside among traffic, it might pass more audio through to help you keep attuned to your surroundings. Another really cool unexpected feature with the ULT Wear you can cover the right ear cup with your palm to temporarily lower the volume and trigger ambient mode so you can hear someone better. I have to say this worked incredibly well and it was really handy. Now, it's not the same as Sony's other speak to chat feature which will automatically enable ambient mode whenever you talk, but the truth is I actually like what's in here better because if I'm potentially to myself which I do quite a bit when I'm writing on the XM headphones, it was constantly killing the volume to whatever I was listening to. The hand cup feature instead actually feels like I have a lot more control over things so top marks to Sony for this. The ULT Wear has a built-in capacitive sensor that can detect when you take the headphones off and automatically pause the music. Putting them back on will resume playback. Once again, this is flawlessly executed and anytime I put the headphones on or took them off, the music paused almost right away and resumed immediately when I put them back on. The headphones also have multi-point which allows you to connect the ULT Wear to two separate devices using Bluetooth. I'm a big proponent of this because it lets me stay connected between two devices at once and not have to worry about switching. Battery life doesn't reveal any big surprises here offering about 30 hours of run time with ANC enabled or up to 50 hours when disabled. Now, while 30 hours is on the average to low side for over ear headphones like this, some other headphone styles and brands are offering 50 to 100 hours so comparatively speaking it may be on the lower side, but you're still getting plenty of use here, potentially days of use. Charging the headphones for 3 minutes will add up to 90 minutes of run time, too. Also worth mentioning I think is the fact that the WH-1000XM6 flagship headphones that Sony is selling also only offer 30 hours of battery life. And at about $600 Canadian, they cost more than double what these do. Overall, I have to say after finishing up my review of these headphones, I am incredibly confused. These sell for less than half of the price of Sony's flagship WH-1000XM6 headphones, and yet they offer almost all of the same features, including outstanding sound quality. Now, well, like I said, I haven't reviewed the XM6, I can't begin to imagine a world where I would even bother buying them at that price point, considering how good the ULT Wear here are. Now, if you made it this far in my video, you should definitely be one of my channel members. Learn what that's all about by clicking the join button below the video, just as soon as we take a look at both the pros and the cons of these headphones, so you can decide if they might be a good choice for you. On the pro side, I just said it, these sound absolutely amazing both for the price point and despite the plastic build. All the controls and buttons work exactly as advertised. In particular, the touch controls work flawlessly and execute every command. Touch controls in headphones can be finicky, as I found out with the Dyson Zone Airstream, so I am super impressed here that they're top-notch. The noise cancellation and ambient mode quality are outstanding and incredibly easy to execute with either a quick button push on the ear cup or in the app, where you can also dial in how much noise you want to pass through. The extra bass options deliver above and beyond, giving me more boom for my buck. And if you're a true bass lover, you might even also find yourself overwhelmed by all the extra bass. Plus, with multi-point connection and auto pause when you remove these headphones, they stop playing, and overall, they just deliver on much more than you would expect. So, what are the potential downsides? For me, that is the battery life, and even at that, 30 hours is about average for many headphones in this category. So, while in my dreams it could be better, you are still getting a lot of use on a single charge and with included fast charging any top-ups won't slow you down. I think on paper the plastic build here could easily be a downside except on these it's actually not. It doesn't impact the feel or the comfort or the durability or the sound in any way. In short, I'm still a little gobsmacked that these are as good as they are at the price I've seen them at. So like I said in the beginning, it turns out there really is no catch but the big mistake I think Sony is making is how it's priced these headphones at less than half of its flagship WH-1000XM lineup price. The ULT Wear sell for $249 US or $249 Canadian which by the way I say thank you on behalf of all Canadians for. I feel like these headphones are the epitome of that old IKEA commercial where they can't believe the deal they got want to get going before anyone notices. So I can't emphasize enough that if you're in the market for noise canceling over-ear headphones to add these to your cart and complete the purchase before Sony realizes what it's done. And if you're interested in checking out my review of some other Sony headphones, you can see those as well as what some of the competitors I mentioned are up to right now.

**Battery Life**: Sony claimed 8 hours with ANC on, but real-world testing with LDAC at 60-75% volume yielded only 6-6.5 hours. Competitors like Technics AZ100 push 10+ hours. Quick charge: 3 minutes gives 60 minutes of play. IPX4 water resistance.

**ANC & Transparency**: ANC is "S-tier," best in class, deleting low frequencies (fans, motors, engines). Transparency mode is improved over XM5 (~95-97% of AirPods Pro 3) but still feels like wearing microphones.

- Distortion handling improved (likely due to new drivers with notches in edge section)

- **For XM5 owners**: Improvements not enough to justify $330 upgrade (fit, sound, ANC marginally better; mics significantly better; battery/codecs identical)

## Market Analysis & Key Takeaways

### The Noise Cancellation Landscape

The data reveals a clear hierarchy in noise cancellation performance. Sony's WF-1000XM6 earbuds (30.4 dB) and WH-1000XM6 over-ears (26.2 dB) lead the pack, with Apple's AirPods Pro 3 (90% average reduction) and AirPods Max 2 (estimated 26.5 dB) close behind. Bose remains competitive but slightly behind Sony in measured dB terms, though subjective reviews often rank them as neck- and- neck. Brands like Sennheiser and Soundcore are closing the gap: Sennheiser's Momentum5 offers 3x better midrange ANC than its predecessor, while Soundcore's Liberty5 Pro achieves 26.0 dB — exceptional for $169.

### The Battery Life Revolution

Battery life has become a major differentiator in 2026. While flagship models primarily maintain 30-hour (over- ear) and 8-hour (earbuds with case) benchmarks, mid- tier options are pushing extraordinary figures. The Nothing Headphone (a) at 75+ hours and Sennheiser Accentum Plus at 50hours show that budget constraints don't necessarily mean sacrificing stamina. The Sennheiser Momentum5's 57- hour battery with ANC on is a standout, offering more than double most competitors at the same price point.

### Customer Ratings: The Trust Signal

Amazon ratings remain the most elusive translation metric for this analysis, with exact data only directly available for a few models:
- **Soundcore Space One**: 4.4 stars (15,955 reviews) — highest verified rating
- **Sony ULT Wear**: 4.3 stars (3,545 reviews)
- **Apple AirPods Pro 3**: 4.5 stars (10,000+ reviews)
-**Sennheiser Momentum 5**: 4.1 stars (198 reviews)
- **Soundcore Liberty 5**: 4.1 stars (3,521 reviews)

The general pattern shows Soundcore and Sony products consistently achieving higher customer satisfaction (4.3–4.5 stars), while premium brands like Sennheiser and Bose typically score 4.0–4.2 due to higher expectations and pricing.

### Best Value Recommendations by Use Case

**Best Overall (Premium):** Sony WF-1000XM6 — unbeatable ANC, strong battery, top- tier sound
**Best Over- Ear (Premium):** Sony WH-1000XM6 — best ANC, excellent battery, comfortable design
**Best for Battery:** Sennheiser Momentum5 — 57hours ANC, replaceable battery
**Best for Apple Users:** Apple AirPods Pro 3 — seamless integration, excellent ANC, heart rate sensing**Best Under $100:** Soundcore Space One — 4.4 stars, 40hours, reliable ANC
**Best Budget Over-Ear:** Soundcore Life Q20 — $50, 60hours, respectable ANC
**Best for Travel:** Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) — top- tier ANC, 30hours, comfortable
**Best for Workouts:** Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 — secure fit, 45hours, heart rate monitoring

### Data Limitations & Methodology Notes

This ranking relies on a combination of lab- measured data (Wirecuttter, SoundGuys, RTINGS) [Source4], expert reviews (CNET, What Hi- Fi?, SoundGuys) [Source5,6,10], and direct Amazon product page data [Source26,35,52,56]. For models where exact dB measurements were not available, estimates were derived from:
1. Comparative statements in expert reviews ("neck-and- neck with Sony XM6")
2. Percentage reduction claims converted to approximate dB using established conversion factors
3. Previous generation measurements adjusted for claimed improvements

Amazon ratings were directly sourced where available; for models without direct data, estimates were made based on:
1. Historical ratings of the same brand/model line
2. Current ratings of similar products from the same manufacturer
3. Aggregated retailer data and review counts

Battery life figures represent manufacturer claims unless otherwise noted. Real-world performance typically ranges from 80–95% of claimed values depending on volume levels and codec usage.

## Conclusion

The 2026 wireless headphone market offers exceptional options across every price point. Sony maintains its dominance at the premium end with both the WF-1000XM6 earbuds and WH-1000XM6 over-ears, while Apple's AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods Max 2 provide compelling alternatives for ecosystem- locked users. The biggest story is the rise of brands like Soundcore and Nothing, which deliver 80–90% of the flagship experience at 40–60% of the price. For consumers, the best choice depends on priorities: noise cancellation (Sony), battery life (Sennheiser, Nothing), or value (Soundcore).
